title: Does overreaching from endurance-based training impair sleep: A systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Murphy C, Svansdottir SA, Dupuy O, Louis J
population: Endurance athletes in overreaching protocols (cycling k=5, rowing 4, triathlon 3, running 2, swimming 1); 14 studies, 3 in the objective and 8 in the subjective meta-analysis
findings: 805 articles returned; 14 studies in the systematic review; overreaching protocols averaged 16 days (range 6 to 28).
Objective sleep (actigraphy, 3 studies): overreaching reduced sleep efficiency (mean difference -2.0%, 95% CI -3.2 to -0.8%; Glass' delta -0.83; p<0.01).
Subjective sleep quality showed no significant effect (Glass' delta -0.27, 95% CI -0.79 to 0.25, p=0.08).
None of the included studies was judged low risk of bias; overreaching from endurance training appears to deteriorate objective sleep without changing perceived sleep quality.
limitations: Only 3 studies in the objective meta-analysis; no study at low risk of bias; short protocols; only 2 running studies.
implications: Use wearable sleep efficiency, not only self-reported sleep quality, as one overreaching signal; a sustained drop of about 2 percentage points versus the athlete's own baseline during a heavy block is consistent with this review but not a validated trigger.
Combine the sleep signal with an efficiency decline or fatigue rating before adding a recovery week; consumer-wearable sleep efficiency is less accurate than actigraphy (not assessed here).

verification.notes: Crossref and PubMed match (PLoS One 2024;19(5):e0303748). Numbers verified in PubMed abstract. Evidence level downgraded A to B: 3 studies, all at non-low risk of bias.
